A patrician is a person who belongs to the highest level of society — someone of noble birth, great wealth, and refined manners who is seen as naturally superior to ordinary people, either by law, tradition, or social standing.

Think of it this way: if society were a building, patricians live on the top floor. Not because they worked their way up — but because they were born there, and the building was essentially built for them.

To truly understand this word, you need to know where it comes from in terms of meaning, because the original meaning is still the primary definition.

In ancient Rome, society was sharply divided into two groups:

  • Patricians — the privileged noble class, made up of a small number of original founding families of Rome.
  • Plebeians — everyone else; the common people, the masses.

This was not just a social distinction. It was a legal one. Patricians had rights and powers that plebeians simply did not have. For much of early Roman history, only patricians could:

  • Hold the highest political offices
  • Serve as priests and interpret religious law
  • Sit in the Senate with full authority
  • Own certain types of land

Being a patrician was not something you could earn. You were either born into a patrician family, or you were not. A plebeian, no matter how rich or talented, could not simply become a patrician. The status was in the bloodline.

This is a critical point: patrician status was inherited, not achieved. That idea — privilege by birth, not effort — is at the very heart of the word.

Today, when someone calls a person a patrician, they usually mean one of two closely related things:

1. A literal aristocrat or member of the upper class.
Someone from an old, established, wealthy family — the kind of family that has had money and status for generations, not just one generation.

"He was a patrician from an old Boston family — his ancestors had been senators and governors."

2. Someone who carries themselves with an air of aristocratic refinement and superiority, even outside a strict class system.

This person is polished, dignified, and composed. They speak carefully. They dress elegantly. They carry a quiet, unspoken sense that they are above the ordinary — and they know it. They may never say it out loud, but it shows in everything they do.

"She had a patrician air about her — calm, measured, and effortlessly superior."
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

This is where it gets nuanced, and this part is important.

The word "patrician" is not always a compliment, and not always a criticism. It depends on context and tone.

  • Used admiringly, it suggests someone has rare dignity, grace, and class.
  • Used critically, it suggests someone is cold, out-of-touch with ordinary people, and has an unearned sense of superiority — someone who looks down on others without justification.

A patrician, in the critical sense, is the kind of person who has never struggled financially, has no idea what it is like to be ordinary, and perhaps doesn't particularly care to know. They inhabit a world of privilege that feels completely natural to them — because for them, it always has been.

The natural opposite of a patrician is a plebeian — the common person, the ordinary person, someone without aristocratic blood or refined airs. Knowing this pair helps cement the meaning:

PatricianPlebeian
Noble classCommon class
Born into privilegeOrdinary origins
Refinement, superiorityEveryday, common
A Few Clear Examples in Sentences

1. "The old patricians of the city controlled its banks, its law firms, and its social clubs for over a century."

→ Here it means the hereditary upper class who held real power.

  1. "He was a patrician in every sense — educated at the finest schools, bred for leadership, and utterly unbothered by the concerns of ordinary life."

→ Here it describes someone whose entire existence is shaped by inherited privilege and refinement.

  1. "There was something patrician about the way she dismissed the question — politely, but with finality, as if the matter were simply beneath serious discussion."

→ Here it captures the manner of a person — superior, composed, and slightly removed from the common world.

A patrician is a member of the noble, privileged upper class — someone who was born into high social standing rather than earning it — and the word also describes anyone who carries themselves with the air of such a person: refined, dignified, and quietly superior.
